prompt.context:
ADSL is a technology that enables the implementation of broadband Internet services via the existing telephony infrastructure. This telephony infrastructure is owned by the incumbent telecom operator in Norway. The regulator has ruled that new entrants may offer ADSL services using the existing incumbent-owned telephony infrastructure via MDF access. This means the new entrant can hire the copper wire from the incumbent operator but has to purchase its own ADSL equipment.

The technical set-up that a new entrant would need basically consists of three elements: MDF access (copper wire), ADSL equipment, and Internet uplink capacity (fiber access connecting the ADSL equipment to the Internet).

The costs involved in establishing the technical set-up are (amounts in Euros):
- MDF access tariff: EUR 12 per line per month (set by the regulator)
- Required investments for ADSL equipment: EUR 120,000 per location, depreciation period of 5 years (linear depreciation, no interest costs). In total, there are 250 locations covering all households in Norway.
- Internet uplink capacity: EUR 2 per end-user per month (on average)
- The consumer ADSL modem is client-owned.
prompt.question: Suppose you wanted to assess if a new entrant can run a profitable business in offering consumer ADSL services — how would you approach this?

clarifying_info.q: What price does the incumbent charge for ADSL services?
clarifying_info.a: The incumbent charges on average EUR 20 per month.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any personnel or overhead costs beyond the technical costs?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. The new entrant has calculated that an annual budget of EUR 4.8 million would be sufficient to cover the entire country for organization and marketing.

clarifying_info.q: How large is the Norwegian household market and what is the current broadband penetration?
clarifying_info.a: There are roughly 2 million households in Norway. Currently: 20% have ADSL services (all with the incumbent), 20% use broadband via cable, 50% still use dial-up, and 10% have no Internet. These percentages were established over the past 5 years (5 years ago no broadband existed). No in-between data is available.

clarifying_info.q: Is the incumbent the only ADSL provider today?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, at the time of this situation, the incumbent operator was the only provider of ADSL services in Norway, though others have considered entering the market.

clarifying_info.q: Is Internet speed proportional to capacity purchased on the uplink?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, the speed you can offer is directly proportional to the capacity you buy and the costs associated with it (i.e., doubling speed doubles the per-user uplink cost).

clarifying_info.q: Are the number of customers per location equal across the country?
clarifying_info.a: No. The area of each region is more or less the same, meaning there is a huge variation in the number of households per location — high-density areas (e.g., Oslo) can cover a much larger share of households through a small fraction of locations.

framework: Start with break-even analysis: since the new entrant has zero customers initially, calculate the minimum number of subscribers needed to cover all fixed and variable costs
Identify revenue driver: price per customer per month (assume parity with incumbent at EUR 20)
Identify variable costs per customer: MDF access (EUR 12/month) + Internet uplink (EUR 2/month) = EUR 14/month => contribution margin = EUR 6/customer/month
Identify fixed costs: ADSL equipment depreciation across all 250 locations + annual organization/marketing budget
Calculate break-even customer count = total monthly fixed costs / contribution margin per customer
Sanity-check the break-even number against market size and realistic achievable share
Assess market growth and competitive dynamics to test whether break-even is achievable
Explore value-creation levers: pricing, service tiers, geographic focus, and product bundling

questions.prompt: Calculate the monthly break-even number of customers for the new entrant, assuming a price of EUR 20/month.
questions.guidance: A strong answer correctly identifies all cost components, computes contribution margin per customer, then divides total monthly fixed costs by that margin. The candidate should flag the need for organizational/marketing cost data before the interviewer volunteers it.

math.setup:
Revenue per customer: EUR 20/month. Variable costs per customer: MDF access EUR 12 + Internet uplink EUR 2 = EUR 14. Contribution margin = EUR 20 - EUR 14 = EUR 6/customer/month.

Fixed costs:
- ADSL equipment: EUR 120,000/location / (5 years x 12 months) = EUR 2,000/location/month. For 250 locations: EUR 2,000 x 250 = EUR 500,000/month.
- Organization & marketing: EUR 4,800,000/year / 12 = EUR 400,000/month.
- Total fixed costs: EUR 500,000 + EUR 400,000 = EUR 900,000/month.
steps: Contribution margin per customer = EUR 20 - EUR 12 - EUR 2 = EUR 6/month
ADSL equipment depreciation per month per location = EUR 120,000 / (5 x 12) = EUR 2,000
Total equipment depreciation = EUR 2,000 x 250 = EUR 500,000/month
Total monthly fixed costs = EUR 500,000 + EUR 400,000 = EUR 900,000

questions.prompt: Is 150,000 customers a realistic target? Use the market data provided to estimate achievable customer numbers over a 5-year horizon.
questions.guidance: The candidate should estimate the addressable pool of new ADSL adopters (currently 50% dial-up = 1,000,000 households most likely to upgrade), project market growth (ADSL doubles from 20% to ~40% of 2M households = 400,000 net new ADSL customers over 5 years), then apply a realistic market share assumption given competition from the incumbent and potential other entrants. The conclusion should be that new customers alone are insufficient to reach break-even.

math.setup:
Total households = 2,000,000. Current ADSL penetration = 20% => 400,000 ADSL customers today (all with incumbent). If ADSL doubles to 40% in 5 years => 800,000 ADSL customers => 400,000 net new ADSL subscribers available.

Market share assumption: incumbent takes >=50% of new customers (strong existing presence). Remaining 50% (200,000) split among 2-3 new entrants => new entrant share of new customers ~17-25% = ~70,000-100,000.
steps: New ADSL subscribers over 5 years = (40% - 20%) x 2,000,000 = 400,000
With 2-3 competing new entrants, one new entrant captures ~17-25% of total new customers
Range: ~70,000-100,000 new customers for the entrant over 5 years
math.answer: The new entrant can realistically attract ~70,000-100,000 new customers from the dial-up segment over 5 years, which falls short of the 150,000 break-even target. Break-even from new customers alone appears unrealistic.

questions.prompt: What is the effect on break-even if the new entrant cuts price by 10% (to EUR 18/month) to attract switching from existing broadband customers?
questions.guidance: The candidate should recalculate contribution margin at the lower price and derive the new break-even, then qualitatively assess whether the incremental switching volume is plausible given high customer satisfaction with the incumbent. The conclusion is that a price cut worsens the economics and is unlikely to generate sufficient switching.

math.setup: New price = EUR 18/month. Variable costs unchanged at EUR 14. New contribution margin = EUR 18 - EUR 14 = EUR 4/month. Fixed costs unchanged at EUR 900,000/month.
steps: New contribution margin = EUR 18 - EUR 14 = EUR 4/customer/month
Break-even rises from 150,000 to 225,000 — a 50% increase — for only a EUR 2 price reduction
math.answer: A 10% price cut raises break-even to 225,000 customers. Given high customer satisfaction with the incumbent, attracting large-scale switching for a EUR 2 discount is unrealistic, and competitors could match the cut, eliminating the advantage.

brainstorming.prompt: The business case looks challenging as structured. What creative ideas could make this business case more attractive?

categories.name: Premium pricing via higher speeds
ideas: Offer a faster/premium ADSL tier at EUR 30/month by doubling Internet uplink capacity (additional EUR 2/user/month cost)
Premium tier increases contribution margin significantly for subscribers who value speed
Diversify into good-better-best pricing tiers to capture different willingness-to-pay segments

categories.name: Service bundling to spread fixed MDF cost
ideas: MDF access costs EUR 12 of the EUR 20 revenue — the largest cost component; bundling additional services over the same copper wire spreads this fixed cost
Add VoIP telephony services over the ADSL connection
Add video/IPTV services if technically feasible
Any additional service re-using the same MDF access dramatically improves unit economics

categories.name: Geographic focus on high-density areas
ideas: Norway's 250 locations have equal geographic area but hugely unequal household density
Start rollout in high-density urban areas (e.g., Oslo and major cities): 20% of locations could cover ~50% of households
Reduces initial ADSL equipment investment by ~80% (from EUR 500,000/month to EUR 100,000/month in depreciation)
Dramatically lowers break-even customer count in the early phase
Expand to lower-density areas only once scale and profitability are proven

categories.name: Target SME / business customers
ideas: Small and medium-sized enterprises in urban areas willing to pay premium prices for reliable broadband
Business customers have higher ARPU and lower churn than residential customers
Enterprise focus aligns with the high-density geographic strategy

categories.name: Cost reduction
ideas: Negotiate volume discounts on Internet uplink capacity as subscriber count grows
Optimize organizational costs by focusing on fewer regions initially
Partner with equipment vendors for more favorable depreciation or lease terms

recommendation: At the current price of EUR 20/month targeting all of Norway, the business case is not viable: break-even requires 150,000 customers but realistic market share yields only ~70,000-100,000 new customers over five years

Recommend a focused entry strategy: launch in high-density urban areas only (e.g., top 20% of locations covering ~50% of households) with a differentiated premium offering at EUR 30/month for higher-speed ADSL targeted at SMEs and premium residential users
This approach dramatically lowers the fixed cost base, raises per-customer contribution margin, and creates a path to break-even within a realistic customer acquisition target
risks: Incumbent responds with price cuts or premium tier launch, eroding the new entrant's competitive position
Other new entrants enter simultaneously, fragmenting the addressable customer base further
Regulatory changes to MDF access tariffs could alter unit economics
Urban high-density focus may trigger incumbent to protect those markets aggressively
Premium pricing strategy may limit addressable market size
next_steps: Model break-even under the high-density + premium pricing scenario to confirm financial viability
Conduct customer research in target urban segments to validate willingness to pay EUR 30 for higher speed
Assess technical feasibility and incremental cost of bundling telephony/video services
Develop phased rollout plan: Phase 1 high-density urban, Phase 2 secondary cities, Phase 3 national coverage
Evaluate capital requirements and funding options for phased equipment rollout
